quiz.question: In Matching Pennies, Player 2 plays $H$ with probability $q=0.6$. What is Player 1's unique best response?

answerOptions.text: Play $T$ for sure ($p=0$), because Player 2 is more likely to play $H$ and Player 1 wants to mismatch.
answerOptions.rationale: Player 1 wins when pennies match, so a high $q$ makes $H$ more attractive, not $T$.

answerOptions.text: Mix fifty-fifty, because Matching Pennies has only a mixed best response.
answerOptions.rationale: Mixing is a best response only at $q=1/2$. For $q\neq 1/2$ there is a unique pure best response.

answerOptions.text: Play $H$ for sure ($p=1$), because $u_1(H,\sigma_2)=2q-1>1-2q=u_1(T,\sigma_2)$ whenever $q>1/2$.
answerOptions.rationale: At $q=0.6$, $u_1(H)=0.2>u_1(T)=-0.2$. Player 1's best-response correspondence puts $p^*=1$ for all $q>1/2$.

answerOptions.text: Any mixture $p\in[0,1]$, because $q$ is close enough to $1/2$ for approximate indifference.
answerOptions.rationale: Indifference holds only at exactly $q=1/2$. Nearby values give a strict ranking of $H$ and $T$.

quiz.question: In a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium of Matching Pennies, Player 1's mixing probability $p^*$ is chosen so that…

answerOptions.text: Player 1 is indifferent between $H$ and $T$ given $p^*$ itself.
answerOptions.rationale: Player 1's indifference depends on $q$, not on $p$. Own mixing does not make oneself indifferent.

answerOptions.text: Player 2 is indifferent between $H$ and $T$.
answerOptions.rationale: The indifference principle says each player's mix makes the opponent willing to mix. Setting $p^*=1/2$ equalises $u_2(H,\sigma_1)$ and $u_2(T,\sigma_1)$.

answerOptions.text: Player 1's mixed strategy strictly dominates both pure strategies.
answerOptions.rationale: The fifty-fifty mix is a best response to $q=1/2$, not a dominant strategy. Against other $q$, a pure strategy does strictly better.

answerOptions.text: Expected payoffs are maximised against every possible $q$, not just the equilibrium $q^*$.
answerOptions.rationale: That would be a dominant strategy. MSNE requires a best response only to the opponent's equilibrium mix.

quiz.hint: Your mix is chosen for the opponent's indifference, not your own.

quiz.question: In Battle of the Sexes ($O,O$: $2,3$; $O,F$: $0,0$; $F,O$: $1,1$; $F,F$: $3,2$), the mixed Nash equilibrium has Player 1 play $O$ with probability $p^*$ and Player 2 play $O$ with probability $q^*$. Which pair is correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Player 2 is indifferent when $1+2p=2-2p$, so $p^*=1/4$. Player 1 is indifferent when $2q=3-2q$, so $q^*=3/4$.
These probabilities are swapped. Each player's mix is set to make the opponent indifferent, not themselves.
Equal mixing is the Matching Pennies equilibrium, not Battle of the Sexes, because payoffs are asymmetric.

answerOptions.text: There is no mixed equilibrium, because two pure equilibria already exist.
answerOptions.rationale: A game can have both PSNE and MSNE. The best-response diagram has a third intersection at $(1/4,3/4)$.

quiz.hint: Set $2q=3-2q$ for Player 1 and $1+2p=2-2p$ for Player 2.

quiz.question: The Battle of the Sexes best-response diagram has three intersections. Which statement is correct?

answerOptions.text: Only the two pure intersections are equilibria; the interior crossing is not a mutual best response.
answerOptions.rationale: At $(p,q)=(1/4,3/4)$ each player is willing to mix, so the interior point is also a Nash equilibrium.

answerOptions.text: The mixed equilibrium Pareto-dominates both pure equilibria because randomisation hedges coordination risk.
answerOptions.rationale: The mixed equilibrium typically yields lower expected payoffs than either coordinated pure equilibrium; mixing does not solve the coordination problem.

answerOptions.text: Generic finite games have an odd number of Nash equilibria, matching the three equilibria here.
answerOptions.rationale: The slide states this general result. Battle of the Sexes has two PSNE and one MSNE, an odd total.

answerOptions.text: Mixed equilibria exist only in games with no pure strategy Nash equilibrium.
answerOptions.rationale: Matching Pennies has MSNE and no PSNE, but Battle of the Sexes has both.

quiz.hint: Count the intersections, including the mixed one.

quiz.question: Why does the existence argument for Nash equilibrium require mixed strategies rather than restricting attention to pure strategies?

answerOptions.text: Mixed strategies make each player's strategy set finite, which is required for Nash's theorem.
answerOptions.rationale: The reverse is true: mixing replaces a finite set of pure strategies with a continuum (the simplex).

answerOptions.text: Without mixing, a player would have no best response to some opponent strategies.
answerOptions.rationale: In a finite game a pure best response always exists (a finite maximum). The problem is convexity of $BR$, not emptiness.

answerOptions.text: Kakutani's theorem requires payoffs to be strictly concave in own mixed strategies.
answerOptions.rationale: Expected payoffs are linear in own mixtures, not strictly concave. Linearity is what makes convex combinations of best responses still best responses.

answerOptions.text: Pure-strategy best-response sets are typically isolated points and need not be convex-valued, violating a Kakutani condition that mixing restores.
answerOptions.rationale: If two pure strategies are both best responses, the pure $BR$ set is two isolated points (not convex). Mixing includes all convex combinations, so $BR_i$ becomes convex-valued.

quiz.question: The keeper improves at blocking shots to the right (save rate $40\%$ to $80\%$). In the new mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, the keeper…

answerOptions.text: Dives right more often, because that action became more productive.
answerOptions.rationale: That is the naive (non-strategic) comparative static. Equilibrium mixing is set to keep the kicker indifferent, not to use the improved action more.

answerOptions.text: Dives right less often ($50\%$ to $30\%$), even though blocking right improved.
answerOptions.rationale: The new indifference conditions give $q^*=\Pr(\text{dive }L)=0.7$, so $\Pr(\text{dive }R)$ falls to $0.3$. The keeper compensates for being better at right by diving there less.

answerOptions.text: Continues to dive fifty-fifty, because the game remains zero-sum.
answerOptions.rationale: Zero-sum structure is unchanged, but the payoff matrix changed, so the minimax mix changes.

answerOptions.text: Stops mixing and always dives right, the newly stronger action.
answerOptions.rationale: A pure strategy of always diving right would be exploited by a kicker who then always goes left. Mixing remains necessary.

quiz.hint: Ask what mix keeps the kicker indifferent after payoffs change.

quiz.question: Why must the improved keeper dive right less often in equilibrium?

answerOptions.text: If they kept diving right as often as before, the kicker would strictly prefer going left, so the original mix would no longer make the kicker indifferent.
answerOptions.rationale: After the right-side improvement, $u_{Ki}(L,q)$ beats $u_{Ki}(R,q)$ at the old $q=1/2$. Raising $q$ (diving left more, right less) restores indifference.

answerOptions.text: Diving right became a strictly dominated strategy once the save rate rose to $80\%$.
answerOptions.rationale: Diving right remains in the support of the new MSNE (played $30\%$ of the time); it is not dominated.

answerOptions.text: The kicker's indifference condition depends only on the kicker's own mixing probability $p$, which rose to $0.7$.
answerOptions.rationale: The kicker's indifference is determined by the keeper's $q$, not by $p$. The rise in $p$ is what keeps the keeper indifferent.

answerOptions.text: Minimax requires each action to be played equally often in every zero-sum game, so the keeper must offset any skill change.
answerOptions.rationale: Minimax need not be fifty-fifty once payoffs are asymmetric. The new mix is $70$-$30$, not equal play.

quiz.hint: Fix $q$ at $1/2$ after the payoff change and compare the kicker's two actions.

quiz.question: In a finite zero-sum game, a player can announce their Nash mixed strategy without lowering their payoff. Why?

answerOptions.text: Because Nash mixed strategies are weakly dominated, so revealing them cannot hurt.
answerOptions.rationale: Equilibrium mixes are best responses, not dominated strategies.

answerOptions.text: Because opponents cannot observe mixed strategies even after they are announced.
answerOptions.rationale: The thought experiment is that the mix is announced and the opponent best-responds. The result is that this does not reduce the value.

answerOptions.text: Because Nash payoffs equal the minimax value: $\max\min u_1=\min\max u_1$, so revealing the minimax mix does not help the opponent exploit you.
answerOptions.rationale: In zero-sum games NE coincides with minimax. The kicker's $50$-$50$ mix guarantees $75\%$ scoring even if the keeper knows it; a $60$-$40$ mix would be exploitable.

answerOptions.text: Because finite zero-sum games have no mixed equilibria, only pure ones.
answerOptions.rationale: Matching Pennies and penalty kicks are finite zero-sum games whose only equilibria are mixed.

quiz.hint: Maxmin equals minmax in zero-sum games.

quiz.question: In an asymmetric matching-pennies hide-and-seek game, MSNE predicts choosing Black about one-third of the time. Students centred near $48\%$ and professional poker players near $50\%$. What is the best interpretation?

answerOptions.text: Poker professionals were closer to theory, confirming that field expertise always transfers to abstract games.
answerOptions.rationale: Professionals centred near $50\%$, no closer to the $33\%$ prediction than students, so expertise did not transfer.

answerOptions.text: The result rejects expected-utility maximisation, because mixing requires non-linear payoffs.
answerOptions.rationale: The lecture does not drop expected utility. The gap is between MSNE play and observed frequencies in an unfamiliar task.

answerOptions.text: Students used minimax while professionals used Nash, which differ in zero-sum games.
answerOptions.rationale: In zero-sum games minimax and Nash coincide, so that distinction cannot explain the two groups.

answerOptions.text: Both groups played Black too often; field expertise did not transfer to this unfamiliar setting.
answerOptions.rationale: Theory is centred near $33\%$; both samples are near $50\%$. The slide takeaway is that expertise in one domain need not produce equilibrium mixing in another.

quiz.hint: Compare both groups to the $33\%$ theoretical benchmark, not to each other.

quiz.question: In capacity-constrained Bertrand, firms mix over prices in $[1/4,1]$. Why must expected profit equal $2$ at every price in the support of the mix?

answerOptions.text: Because market demand is $10$ and each firm has capacity $8$, so residual demand of $2$ is the equilibrium quantity.
answerOptions.rationale: Residual demand of $2$ is what a firm sells when undercut; it is not why expected profit is constant across the support.

answerOptions.text: By the indifference principle: every price played with positive probability must yield the same expected profit, equal to the sure profit from pricing at $1$.
answerOptions.rationale: Pricing at $1$ yields profit $2$ for sure. Any $p$ in the support of a mixed best response must match that payoff, which pins down $F(p)=(4p-1)/(3p)$.

answerOptions.text: Because undercutting always yields profit $8$, which averaged with zero profit gives $2$.
answerOptions.rationale: Undercutting yields $8p$, not $8$, and a firm that prices above the rival still sells $2$ units, not zero.

answerOptions.text: Because Nash's theorem requires equilibrium payoffs of $2$ in every finite pricing game.
answerOptions.rationale: Existence says nothing about the payoff level $2$; that number is the outside option of pricing at the choke price $1$.

quiz.hint: What payoff must every strategy in the support of a mixed best response deliver?
